body.heading: A butterfly that answers a balloon
paragraphs: This little butterfly cannot fly — its wings are tissue paper. But bring a rubbed balloon close and the wings lift and flutter as if it were alive. No strings, no magnets, no touching. The puppeteer is invisible: static electricity.

body.heading: Meet the parts
paragraphs: The wings — two shapes cut from a single layer of tissue paper, light enough for a whisper of force to lift. The body — a strip of card the wings are glued along, like a real butterfly's body. The garden — a piece of cardboard the butterfly rests on. The charger — a balloon, rubbed on hair or a woolly jumper to load it with static.

body.heading: You will need
paragraphs: Tissue paper, a small strip of card, a piece of cardboard for the garden, safety scissors, a glue stick, crayons for decorating, and one balloon — which a grown-up inflates, ties and keeps in charge of.

body.heading: How it works — step by step
paragraphs: Step 1 — Cut the wings. Fold the tissue in half and cut a wing shape so you get two matching wings joined at the fold. Tissue tears easily — slow scissors win.

Step 2 — Build the butterfly. Glue just the fold line to the card body — the wings themselves stay free and floppy. Draw a face and spots if you like, and glue the body to the middle of the cardboard garden.
Step 3 — Charge the balloon. Your grown-up rubs the balloon briskly on clean, dry hair or a wool jumper, about ten rubs. The balloon is now carrying an invisible electric charge.

Step 4 — Bring the balloon slowly down toward the butterfly — close, but not touching. The wings rise to meet it and flutter! Move the balloon away and they settle. Closer, and they lift again. You are conducting with static.

body.heading: The science bit
paragraphs: Rubbing moves tiny electric charges onto the balloon — this build-up is called static electricity. The charged balloon attracts light, uncharged things: the tissue wings are pulled toward it, just as charged balloons pull hair and tiny paper bits. It is the same force that makes a crackle when you pull off a jumper — and, in a giant sky-sized version, lightning.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Why do the wings fall back down when the balloon moves away?
2. The trick works best on a dry day. Why do you think rainy, damp air makes static tricks weaker?

takeaway: Rubbing gives a balloon a static electric charge, and that charge attracts light things — strong enough to lift a tissue butterfly's wings without touching them.
materials: Safety scissors and a glue stick
One balloon — inflated and tied by a grown-up
supervision: A grown-up inflates, ties and holds charge of the balloon, and supervises the whole activity.
safetyNotes: BALLOON RULES: grown-ups inflate balloons — never children. Keep balloons away from faces while inflating, and if one pops, pick up every piece at once: burst balloon pieces are a serious choking hazard for babies, toddlers and pets.
Children with a latex allergy should do this build with a rubbed plastic ruler instead — ask your grown-up first.
Static is gentle, but never rub a balloon near anyone's eyes or ears, and stop if the popping sounds worry a younger child — watch from a happy distance instead.
screenFreeExtension: Static parade: test what else the charged balloon can lift — tiny paper stars, a thread, a trickle of water from a tap (grown-up at the sink). Rank them from easiest to hardest to lift.
